title: Which road next?
kid: A router reads the address label on every parcel and checks its signposts: which road takes it closer to that address? Then off the parcel goes, down that road.
nerd: A router looks up the destination in its forwarding table. The longest matching prefix wins (a /24 beats the default route 0.0.0.0/0), the TTL goes down by one, and the packet leaves on that route’s interface.

describe.kid: A paper road links your device, this router and the video server. One card shows the parcel’s address label. Another card is a post with road signs. A walking parcel stops here, a magnifying glass reads the label, one sign glows, and the parcel walks on.
describe.nerd: The close-up shows the IP header with From, To and TTL. The router’s signs show a client prefix and a default or server route. When the packet pauses, the destination row lights up. Longest-prefix match chooses a sign, TTL counts down, and the packet leaves.

nat.title: The swap notebook
nat.kid: Everything at home shares one outside address. The home router swaps the sender sticker for its own address and writes it in its notebook, so when the answer comes back it knows who asked.
nat.nerd: NAPT: the private source address and port are rewritten to the public address. The mapping (inside address:port ↔ outside port) stays in the connection table, and replies are matched on it and rewritten back.

describe.kid: A road links your devices, the home router and the video server. The address card changes the From sticker to the router. The swap notebook lists you and another device with ticket numbers. The parcel pauses at the router, the label changes, and replies come back through the notebook.
describe.nerd: The close-up shows the IP source being rewritten beside the NAT table. Rows map the inside host and port to an outside port. The active row appears and glows on the return leg. The packet keeps moving, with TTL counted down like any routed hop.

bridge.title: Just passing through
bridge.kid: This box doesn’t even read the address label! It takes off the envelope the parcel came in and puts on a new one for the next stretch.
bridge.nerd: A layer-2 device (or one that tunnels): it strips the incoming link frame and writes a new one for the outgoing link, with new MAC addresses. The IP header, TTL included, is never touched.

describe.kid: A road links your device, this passing box and the video server. The address card has sleepy eyes, and the other card shows the old and new envelopes. The parcel keeps its address label closed while one envelope lifts away and a fresh one drops on for the next stretch.
describe.nerd: The IP header card is shown but not read. The link card shows incoming and outgoing envelopes. Technical labels mention a new MAC address and an untouched IP header. During the pause, the old layer-2 frame lifts off, the new frame lands, and the packet continues with the same IP label and TTL.

endpoint.title: Is it for me?
endpoint.kid: At the end of the road the computer checks the address label against its own address. It’s a match! It opens the parcel and hands the numbered piece inside up. On everything it sends, it writes the label itself.
endpoint.nerd: The destination matches a local address, so the IP header is stripped and the payload goes up to TCP (protocol 6). For outgoing packets the host writes the source, the destination and a fresh TTL of 64.

describe.kid: The road ends at the device being checked. One card shows the address label, and another shows the device’s own address like a door plate. A parcel arrives, the label matches, and a small numbered piece rises to the next layer. On the way out, the label is written before the parcel leaves.
describe.nerd: At an endpoint, the IP header is compared with the local address on the plate. The incoming payload rises toward the next layer. On the outgoing leg, the host writes a fresh source, destination and TTL 64. Labels show protocol 6 to TCP and new packets with TTL 64.

mobile-core.title: A whole street shares one address
mobile-core.kid: Phones on the mobile network don’t get an internet address of their own. The mobile core swaps the sender sticker of lots of phones for the same single address, and gives each its own ticket number in its notebook.
mobile-core.nerd: Carrier-grade NAT: subscribers get addresses from the shared space 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598), and thousands of them share one public IPv4 address, each with its own block of ports. This is a big reason for IPv6.

describe.kid: The road shows several phones sharing a mobile core on the way to the video server. The address card changes From to Mobile core. The swap notebook is full of neighbours with ticket numbers. A parcel stops at the core, gets its sticker changed, then walks on. Replies use the notebook to find the right phone.
describe.nerd: This is the NAT variant for carrier-grade NAT. The card rewrites a source from 100.64.0.0/10 to the carrier’s public address. The table maps several inside address and port pairs to outside ports. The packet pauses for the rewrite, TTL drops, and forwarding continues.
